clinicalPearls: Large deletions in the beta-globin gene cluster remove both the delta and beta genes, so neither HbA2 nor HbA is produced normally from the affected chromosome.
Compensatory gamma-chain output rises, producing the characteristic raised fetal haemoglobin (HbF).
In heterozygous (trait) form the HbA2 is normal or low — the key feature separating it from beta-thalassaemia trait, in which HbA2 is raised.
Homozygotes typically show a thalassaemia intermedia picture, milder than beta-thalassaemia major, because the abundant HbF is protective.
The blood film shows microcytic, hypochromic red cells with the changes of thalassaemia.
Distinguish from hereditary persistence of fetal haemoglobin, where HbF distribution is pancellular and there is little or no anaemia or microcytosis.
Hb Lepore, arising from a delta-beta fusion gene, produces a similar clinical picture and should be considered.
The cellular distribution of HbF (heterocellular versus pancellular) on Kleihauer testing or flow cytometry helps classify the disorder.
reference.pathophysiology: The beta-globin gene cluster on chromosome 11 contains, in order, the embryonic, fetal (Gg and Ag), delta and beta genes under the control of the locus control region. In delta-beta thalassaemia, large deletions remove both the delta and beta genes, and often part of the gamma region, abolishing delta- and beta-chain synthesis from the affected chromosome. Loss of beta-chain production creates the imbalance of globin chains and the ineffective erythropoiesis typical of thalassaemia, but the same deletions also remove regulatory elements that normally silence the gamma genes after birth, so gamma-chain synthesis persists and rises. The resulting abundant HbF (a2g2) partly compensates for the missing HbA (a2b2), which is why homozygotes have a comparatively mild intermedia phenotype and heterozygotes are usually only mildly affected. Because the delta gene is also deleted, HbA2 (a2d2) is not increased, distinguishing the trait from classical beta-thalassaemia trait.
additionalDifferentials: Beta-thalassaemia trait (raised HbA2) and beta-thalassaemia intermedia or major
Iron deficiency anaemia (microcytic, but with distinct HbF and HbA2 patterns)
Other conditions with raised HbF such as some acquired marrow disorders and juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia
Compound inheritance with sickle cell disease, which modifies severity
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film showing microcytosis and hypochromia
Haemoglobin electrophoresis or high-performance liquid chromatography quantifying HbF, HbA2 and HbA
Kleihauer test or flow cytometry to assess the cellular distribution of HbF
Iron studies and ferritin to exclude coexisting iron deficiency
DNA analysis of the beta-globin cluster for deletions and for Hb Lepore
Family studies with parental haemoglobin analysis
redFlags: Marked anaemia or transfusion dependence suggesting a more severe genotype or compound inheritance
Features of iron overload despite limited or no transfusion, as seen in intermedia phenotypes
Growth failure or skeletal changes in a child implying more severe thalassaemia
Symptomatic anaemia developing during pregnancy or intercurrent illness
reference.prognosis: Generally favourable — heterozygotes are only mildly affected and homozygotes usually follow a thalassaemia intermedia course; the main long-term concern is iron overload, particularly where transfusion or increased gastrointestinal iron absorption occurs.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the trait as beta-thalassaemia trait; the normal or low HbA2 is the discriminator.
Confusing it with hereditary persistence of fetal haemoglobin without checking HbF cellular distribution and red-cell indices.
Overlooking coexisting iron deficiency, which can alter the HbA2 and HbF picture.
Prescribing unnecessary long-term iron for a microcytosis that is not due to iron deficiency.
Failing to offer genetic counselling and partner testing to assess antenatal risk.
